<reason>This was a closely fought, well-matched debate with both sides honoring the format. Side A built a coherent structural case (recurring costs vs. one-off payments, Nordic/French infrastructure, the motherhood penalty) and landed real hits: the "rent arrears" concession gotcha and the completed-cohort-fertility metric. But Side B consistently fought on East Asian ground, which is what the motion specifies: Singapore's solved-housing/lowest-fertility case, Japan/Korea's daycare expansion with record-low births, and provincial cities with cheap homes all directly undercut the PRO lever, while A's best natural experiment (Nordics/France) is non-East Asian and was blunted by "sliding in real time." B also exploited A's own concession that work hours and gender norms—not housing or childcare—are the real drivers, framing PRO as needing "a labor revolution plus a gender revolution plus a housing boom" while CON "needs an envelope." A's sharpest attack—timing effects are borrowed births—was met with a genuinely responsive mechanism: in East Asia, postponement frequently becomes permanent childlessness, so pulling births forward rescues rather than reshuffles them; A's "lottery ticket" retort was rhetorical but not a full neutralization. Both sides answered pressure questions directly with A1/A2 structure. B's minor cost is some asserted specificity ("lifted second-birth shares") without grounding, but A matched it with the unsupported "none exists." Net: B's case stayed truer to the East Asian comparison and survived A's best pressure slightly better.</reason>
<best_rebuttal>The decisive exchange was the timing clash: A's "borrowed births" argument (a birth pulled from 35 to 31 is rescheduled, not created) against B's reply that East Asian delay-to-35 often becomes zero births, so pulling births forward rescues completed fertility that postponement would erase. A never fully answered this beyond calling it a "lottery ticket," leaving B's mechanism standing.</best_rebuttal>
